endorsements.title: Marketing Submission Recommendations for a Predetermined Change Control Plan for AI-Enabled Device Software Functions (final guidance)
endorsements.quote: The impact assessment section of a PCCP should include an assessment of the benefits and risks of implementing a PCCP for a device, as well as documentation of associated risk mitigations.

commentary.bottom_line: FDA final guidance on predetermined change control plans asks manufacturers to assess the benefits and risks of each planned modification and of the plan as a whole, and to document the associated risk mitigations. No study supplied here tests whether this assessment prevents unrecognized risks from individual or combined modifications, so the recommendation rests on regulatory expectation rather than measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: No study in this map tests the practice, and no study documents the hazard of unrecognized risk from single or combined modifications. Under GRADE conventions, certainty about the effect of benefit-risk impact assessment on patient outcomes or device performance cannot be rated. The single endorsement is a guidance document, which reflects expert and regulatory judgment rather than empirical evidence.

The FDA final guidance places the benefit-risk assessment and documentation of mitigations in the impact assessment section of a predetermined change control plan. For manufacturers seeking an authorized plan, this functions as a submission expectation. The guidance uses "should" language, and its content describes what reviewers expect to see rather than evidence that the assessment reduces harm.

commentary.research_gap: No study has examined whether documented benefit-risk assessments within change control plans identify risks that would otherwise go unrecognized, particularly risks arising from the interaction of several modifications. Useful studies could compare postmarket performance, adverse event reports, or field corrections for AI-enabled devices modified under plans with differing depth of impact assessment, and could test whether assessments of combined modifications detect performance shifts in subgroups that single-modification assessments miss.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. It remains unknown whether manufacturers' benefit-risk assessments account for how modifications may change device performance in these groups, and health systems serving them cannot rely on published evidence that the assessments protect their patients.
